extracted.intended_audience: students of literature, literary critics, and aspiring novelists
extracted.subtask_description: Lecture-style guidance on how to read, evaluate, and think about novels by isolating distinct 'aspects' (story, people, plot, fantasy, prophecy, pattern, rhythm) and applying critical standards and examples. Aimed to teach literary judgment and practical criteria for critique and creation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duties of the critic (T. S. Eliot)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘It is part of his business to preserve tradition—when a good tradition exists. It is part of his business to see literature steadily and to see it whole; and this is eminently to see it not as consecrated by time, but to see it beyond time.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should (when possible) preserve good tradition, aim to see literature steadily and as a whole, and strive to judge works beyond the accidents of their date. The lecturer notes practical limits (e.g., lack of reading prevents preserving tradition) but endorses the ideal of viewing novelists across time and place rather than chronologically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final test — reader's affection
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The final test of a novel will be our affection for it…’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The lecturer claims that ultimately a novel's success is judged by the reader's emotional attachment—liking or affection—while warning against uncritical sentimentality. Critics should allow personal response but keep sentimentality from dominating early judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Story
rubrics_metrics.description: Defined as 'a narrative of events arranged in their time sequence.' The story is the fundamental, primitive aspect of the novel: the backbone or 'tape-worm' that makes the audience want to know what happens next.
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
Key evaluative points and guidance in the text:
- A story's sole merit: making the audience want to know what happens next; its sole fault: making the audience not want to know.
- Story appeals to 'primeval curiosity' and is often judged intolerantly or unreasonably by readers who favor it.
- Devices that sustain story interest include suspense (illustrated by Scheherazade) and natural scene-setting/introduction of characters (Scott's technique).
- Story is distinct from plot (the plot is a 'higher' organism) and from other novel aspects (people, pattern, etc.).
- Time-sequence is intrinsic: a novelist cannot entirely abolish chronological sequence without rendering fiction unintelligible; experiments (Brontë, Sterne, Proust) may alter or play with time but do not negate the necessity of temporal structure. Gertrude Stein's attempt to abolish time is judged a failure on this ground.
- The story is especially suited to oral reading: it conveys a voice and benefits from being read aloud; it transforms readers into listeners.
- Anti-patterns: overcelebrating mere chronological succession (leading to shallowness), using marriage as an idiotic finale, or substituting patchwork episodes without sufficient emotional or intellectual grounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: People (characters)
rubrics_metrics.description: The actors in the novel—'word-masses' describing human beings—intended to reveal inner life as well as outward actions; the novelist can create characters more fully 'understandable' than in real life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
Principles and guidance from the lecture:
- Novelistic characters differ from historical persons: historians infer character from actions; novelists may invent inner lives and intentions beyond observable evidence.
- The novelist conditions characters by temperament and by other aspects of the work (plot, setting, etc.). Characters may be created deliriously, but their nature is shaped by what the novelist guesses about others and himself.
- Alain's view (paraphrased): the novel reveals the 'romanesque' side of people—their pure passions, dreams, sorrows and inner soliloquies—that politeness or shame might hide in real life. Thus what is 'fictitious' is often the method by which thought develops into action.
- Practical checkpoint: consider how the novelist treats the five main facts of human life (birth, food, sleep, love, death)—does the novelist reproduce them accurately, exaggerate, minimize, or transform them?
- Anti-patterns: making characters mere copies of real persons (turning the novel into a memoir) or failing to provide inner life and intentionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Mentioned as one of the seven aspects; distinguished from the story as 'an organism of a higher type' that will be defined later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot is signalled as a more complex, higher-level organization than simple chronological story. The lecturer promises fuller definition and discussion in subsequent lectures; the present guidance is to treat plot as an organizing principle beyond mere time-sequence, responsible for cause, design, and artistic unity rather than simple event succession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fantasy
rubrics_metrics.description: Listed among the seven aspects selected for discussion (The Story; People; The Plot; Fantasy; Prophecy; Pattern and Rhythm).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The lecture identifies fantasy as a distinct aspect through which a novelist may look at his work or vice versa. In this chunk the author only lists it; further lectures are implied to elaborate how imagination/speculative elements function in novels and how they should be judged (e.g., their sincerity, role in meaning-making, relation to plausibility).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophecy
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the seven named aspects of the novel to be examined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Though not expanded here, 'prophecy' is presented as an evaluative dimension—how far a novel contains visionary or prognostic elements about humanity or society. Future discussion (elsewhere in the lectures) would treat how prophetic content contributes to a novel's significance or fails by being either too didactic or unintelligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: Named as one of the seven aspects (Pattern) to be discussed in relation to the novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pattern refers to the structural, recurring, or arranging relationships in a novel (e.g., thematic repetition, symmetry, distribution of incidents). In this chunk it is only listed; the implication is that critics should evaluate the coherence and aesthetic arrangement of elements across a work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhythm
rubrics_metrics.description: Listed among the seven aspects of the novel (Pattern and Rhythm).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rhythm concerns cadence, tempo, pacing and the musical qualities of prose and narrative flow. The lecture notes that some aspects (like melody or cadence) can be apprehended by the eye as well as the ear, but rhythm as an aspect will be treated later; critics should attend to pacing, sentence and paragraph rhythm, and how these contribute to the novel's overall effect.
